comparison: Perfect agreement on experimental design (C4, C39, C45-C56). Both evaluations found the two-phase training protocol well-designed and supported. Peer reviewers praised it as 'elegant' and 'well worked out,' matching OpenEval's assessment that methodology is clearly documented with appropriate controls.

Strong agreement on behavioral learning results (C57-C80, C192-C197). Both evaluations accepted the lick index metric and learning trajectories without challenge. OpenEval found differential salience well-supported; peer reviewers noted the distractor stimulus findings were convincing, though requested clearer quantification in figure legends.

Complete agreement on recording methodology (C81-C89). Both evaluations found electrophysiology methods appropriate with adequate quality control. Peer reviewers called methods 'state-of-the-art' and 'well executed,' consistent with OpenEval's assessment of appropriate technical details and validation.

Strong agreement on POm electrophysiological findings (C6, C41, C90-C97, C106). Both evaluations accepted the heterogeneity and modality-specific responses as well-documented. Peer reviewers found the case 'compelling' that POm neurons are less modality-specific than assumed, matching OpenEval's support.

Agreement on POm conditioning-dependent plasticity (C7, C42, C98-C103). Both evaluations accepted the dramatic plasticity findings. OpenEval and peer reviewers both found the quantitative evidence for population response changes compelling, supporting the main conclusion about cross-modal activation.

Divergence on latency interpretation (C107-C122). OpenEval found the latency analysis well-supported with clear evidence that early responses remain constant while late responses change. However, Peer Reviewer 3 questioned whether 40ms latencies represent 'purely sensory' responses and requested dampened conclusions about responses 'to the onset' of stimuli.

Agreement on movement/arousal regression analysis (C8, C123-C144). Both evaluations accepted that the regression approach appropriately addresses behavioral confounds. Peer Reviewer 1 explicitly accepted that cross-modal short latency responses are not clearly related to animal behavior, consistent with OpenEval's assessment.

Agreement on overlap between movement and stimulus tuning (C145-C148). Both evaluations accepted the linear model approach showing high percentages of dual-tuned cells. This finding was incorporated into peer reviewers' acceptance of the regression analysis controlling for movement.

Complete agreement on spatial analysis (C9, C149-C160). Both evaluations accepted the selectivity index metric and histological localization showing a core whisker-sensitive region. Peer reviewers noted the functional heterogeneity has been suggested in earlier studies and accepted the spatial findings.

Agreement on LP findings parallel to POm (C10, C43, C161-C171, C185). Both evaluations accepted LP activity reshaping by conditioning. Peer reviewers treated LP data as supporting the main conclusion about secondary thalamic nuclei, consistent with OpenEval's assessment of parallel findings.

Agreement on LP temporal dynamics (C172-C178). Both evaluations accepted the detailed temporal analysis showing early visual responses only in tactilely conditioned mice and conditioning-dependent changes in late responses, supporting the broader LP findings.

Agreement on LP control analyses (C179-C184). Both evaluations accepted the movement correction showing persistence of air puff responses. The limited spatial sampling acknowledged by authors was not challenged by peer reviewers, matching OpenEval's assessment.

Strong agreement on main conclusions (C11-C12, C44, C186-C191, C278-C279). Both evaluations strongly supported the conclusion that behavioral training reshapes secondary thalamic nuclei. Editor and reviewers found evidence 'compelling,' matching OpenEval's assessment that conclusions are well-supported by comprehensive data.

Agreement on task structure effects on learning (C192-C197). Both evaluations accepted behavioral findings about differential learning rates and stimulus salience. These claims were incorporated into peer reviewers' broader acceptance of behavioral results.

OpenEval rated interpretation of salience differences (C198-C201) as UNCERTAIN due to speculative claims about personal space and uncited human perception claims. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addressed these interpretive claims.

Partial overlap on mechanistic interpretation (C202-C209). OpenEval found anatomical interpretation supported and appropriately cautious about sensory versus attention-related responses. Peer reviewers raised broader questions about whether responses reflect attention versus sensory processing, noting the origin of cross-modal responses remains open.

OpenEval found integration with prior literature and modality-specific sensitization interpretation (C210-C216) supported by differential licking correlations. No specific peer review evaluation addressed these particular interpretive claims.

OpenEval rated correlational findings and mechanistic interpretations (C217-C221) as UNCERTAIN, noting speculative interpretations about visual sensitivity versus arousal not directly tested. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addressed these claims.

OpenEval found LP mechanistic interpretation (C222-C232) supported by anatomical knowledge and appropriately cautious speculation. No specific peer review evaluation addressed these particular LP interpretation claims separately from general LP findings.

OpenEval found acknowledgment of LP spatial sampling limitations (C233-C236) appropriate and speculation about other subregions reasonable. Peer reviewers acknowledged limited LP coverage but did not separately evaluate these specific limitation claims.

Both rated neuromodulation hypotheses (C237-C245) as speculative. OpenEval marked UNCERTAIN noting no direct measurements performed. Peer reviewers similarly noted mechanistic origins remain 'an open question' requiring future investigation, though did not specifically evaluate neuromodulation claims separately.

Both rated alternative mechanisms (C246-C252) as speculative. OpenEval marked UNCERTAIN noting mechanisms not directly tested. Peer reviewers raised questions about specificity and what aspects of the task POm/LP respond to, indicating mechanistic interpretations remain unresolved.

Both rated functional role in cortico-cortical communication (C253-C257) as speculative. OpenEval marked UNCERTAIN noting no direct measurement of cortico-cortical communication. Peer reviewers noted the origin of cross-modal responses requires future investigation.

OpenEval found contextualization within primate attention literature (C258-C266) well-justified and appropriately identifying novel contributions. No specific peer review evaluation separately addressed these literature comparison claims.

Both rated functional role predictions (C267-C277) as speculative. OpenEval marked UNCERTAIN noting predictions about plasticity windows and disruption effects not directly tested. Peer reviewers' questions about task specificity and attention mechanisms align with uncertainty about these broader functional predictions.
